newsitem.title: BANGLADESH: FEATURE-Bangladesh port privatisation plan hits snag.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE-Bangladesh port privatisation plan hits snag.

text.p: Angry workers and employees held the chairman of Chittagong Port Authority (CPA) hostage in his office last month as jubilant comrades outside reinforced the siege and halted cargo handling.
Labour unrest has hit Bangladesh's main port ever since the government decided to end the state monopoly in cargo handling.

Chittagong Mayor Mohammad Mohiuddin rescued CPA chairman Zahiruddin Mahmood after seven hours and calmed the workers. He also told the government to accept their demands, including wage rises and dropping the plan to privatise cargo handling, or face a shutdown.

"We want scrapping of the agreement with the private sector for cargo handling. The port authority should do necessary expansion of the port from its own resources," said one leader of the port labour union.

The unrest signals a greater anti-privatisation campaign ahead for the government of Prime Minister Sheikh Hasina, which came to power after a general election in June. Her government has pledged to pursue a free-market economy and end state controls.
Mahmood appeared helpless as he forecast difficult tasks ahead. Port users say everything has been held up by its public employees.
"The port workers will not lose (their) jobs by the privatisation drive. Their policy of not allowing private sector work is suicidal," Mahmood told Reuters.
"We have a plan to ease the state monopoly. Port authorities are leasing out some activities to private companies," he said.
HUGE PRESSURE ON PORT CAPACITY SEEN
Mahmood sees huge pressure on the limited capacity of the country's prime sea port and suggests it be expanded extensively to cope with the future load.

He said if Bangladesh would provide transit facilities to neighbouring countries the port's cargo trade would increase many times. Land-locked Nepal has been using Chittagong port for a long time and India and Bhutan, also a land-locked country, have shown interest in using it as well.
But Mahmood was uncertain about the future of the port. A jetty extension plan, prepared four years ago, has been shelved.
"The World Bank wants the extension (ownership) to be given to private hands. But we feel two of the four jetties planned should go to the private parties," he said.
"There is also a funding problem. The two jetties will cost seven billion taka ($165 million). Bangladesh is seeking foreign assistance" for the project, he added.
Mahmood said the port has seven terminals but needs two more. It handles 11.5 million tonnes of cargo annually, including four million tonnes shipped in containers.
Mohsin Sarker, director (traffic) of the port authority, said the government planned a dedicated container terminal to ease pressure on the port.

"There has been a decision to build the terminal under a BOT (build-operate-transfer) system. The World Bank may finance the project and it is now studying the project. It may take at least one year time to call a tender," he said.
"We also want to introduce some five gantry cranes - four of which will be ship-to-shore and one yard gantry -- under private sector initiatives," he said.
RESTIVE LABOUR FORCE CAUSING DELAYS
"(But) I don't think the government will be able to go ahead with its planned programme...because of the restive labour force," said M. Amirul Haque, managing director of Seacom Ltd.
"The labour union will not allow the private sector to operate in the port. There will be a serious deadlock."

Seacom Ltd comprises Seacom Shipping Ltd, Seacom Containers Ltd and Seacom Corp Ltd. The firm, which has annual turnover of more than $80 million, owns three ocean-going vessels with total capacity of 53,390 tonnes.
Haque said the port labour union had prevented the authority from using four straddle carriers brought in by a private company that won the contract through a bidding.

"There are other problems, too. Ships with rice are idling for months at the port on grounds of a quality dispute. Ships have no responsibility for quality and that's the matter between suppliers and importers," he said.

Haque said there has been "unnecessary" delays in checking cargo, especially grains, by customs officials before making assessment on duties. "There are many other reasons to keep ships stranded for several days," he said.
International ship owners have already warned of making Bangladesh ports an "exclusion zone" for their ships, especially those carrying grain, he said without giving details.
